title: Can salty water help corals survive a heatwave?
blurb: Corals turn white when the sea gets too hot. Tiny sea anemones kept in saltier water lost less colour, a clue to the tough corals of the Red Sea.

cover.alt: Drawings and photos of tiny sea anemones after heat: see-through in low salt, brownest in high salt, with a bar chart
cover.credit: Figure 2, Gegner and Voolstra, Frontiers for Young Minds, CC BY 4.0

source.name: Frontiers for Young Minds
source.title: A Salty Coral Secret: How High Salinity Helps Corals To Be Stronger
source.authors: Hagen M. Gegner, Christian R. Voolstra

original.title: High salinity conveys thermotolerance in the coral model Aiptasia
original.authors: Hagen M. Gegner, Maren Ziegler, Nils Rädecker, Carol Buitrago-López, Manuel Aranda, Christian R. Voolstra

cards.b: Corals are animals that build reefs. Tiny algae, which are water plants, live inside corals and give them food and colour. When the sea gets too hot, corals lose their algae and turn white. This is called bleaching. Yet corals in the Red Sea cope with very hot water, and the Red Sea is also very salty. Could the salt be part of their secret?

Hagen Gegner did this research for his PhD, a university research degree, in Saudi Arabia. He worked with Christian Voolstra and their colleagues. Christian studies how animals and plants team up with tiny living things. They published the study in 2017.

Corals are hard to keep in a lab. So the team used Aiptasia, a tiny sea anemone. Anemones are soft sea animals, close cousins of corals, and they carry the same algae. The team kept them in low, medium or high salt water at 25°C. Then they heated half of each group to 34°C for 8 days and counted the algae left inside.

img.alt: A drawing comparing the simple cell layers of a coral and an Aiptasia anemone, with algae living inside
img.credit: Figure 1, Gegner and Voolstra, Frontiers for Young Minds, CC BY 4.0

cards.b: All the heated anemones bleached, but not equally. In low salt water, only about 14 of every 100 algae stayed. In medium salt about 31 stayed, and in high salt about 37. So the saltiest water protected them best. The photos agreed. High-salt anemones stayed brownish, and low-salt ones went see-through.

This was one experiment, on anemones, not on real corals. The team does not yet know how the salt helps. One idea is that in salty water, the animals make more molecules called osmolytes. These balance the salt in their cells. Osmolytes may also clean up harmful molecules made during heat. Next the team plans to test real Red Sea corals.

img.alt: A cherry split open after rain, and a diagram of water moving towards the sugary side, which is called osmosis
img.credit: Figure 3, Gegner and Voolstra, Frontiers for Young Minds, CC BY 4.0

cards.b: Coral reefs are colourful homes for sea life, and they are in danger as the oceans warm up quickly. Not all corals bleach at the same temperature. Finding out why some corals are tougher could help scientists understand bleaching and look after reefs.

See salt pull water out. Put a cucumber slice in a bowl of plain water. Put another in very salty water, made with three big spoons of salt in one cup of water. After 30 minutes, bend each slice gently. The salty one is floppy, because salt pulled water out of its cells. Animals in very salty seas have the same problem. The team thinks osmolytes may help balance it.

Red Sea corals live in hot, salty water and seem tougher for it. Should people make reefs saltier to protect them? Or should we first find out exactly why salt helps? What could go wrong if we changed the sea?

words.m: when corals lose their algae in hot water and turn white
tiny water plants that make food from sunlight
a soft sea animal, a close cousin of corals, with no skeleton
